messages.content: I just got a dispute notification for charge ch_3Xyz — $127.50. The reason says 'product not received' but my tracking clearly shows it was delivered. I've never dealt with a chargeback before. What do I do?

Hi Maya — I can see the dispute on charge ch_3Xyz for $127.50 with the reason 'product not received.' Here's what you need to know and do right away.

A dispute (also called a chargeback) means the cardholder has asked their card issuer to reverse the payment. You have a limited window to respond — typically 7 to 21 days depending on the card network — so acting quickly is important. If you don't respond before the deadline, you automatically lose the dispute.

Because your tracking shows the item was delivered, you have strong evidence. Here's what to gather:
• Shipping confirmation and tracking number
• Proof of delivery (carrier confirmation screenshot or photo)
• Any customer communication records (emails, messages)
• Order details showing the item description and fulfillment date

Once you have these ready, you can submit your response directly in your Stripe Dashboard under the Disputes tab. I've opened a case for you (CAS-2026-00391) and pre-filled it with your dispute reason and charge ID. Would you like step-by-step instructions for submitting in the Dashboard?

messages.content: Yes please. I have the tracking number and a screenshot of the delivery confirmation from the carrier. Is that enough to win?

Great — that's exactly the right evidence for a 'product not received' dispute. Here's how to submit it in your Stripe Dashboard:

1. Log in to your Stripe Dashboard and go to Payments > Disputes.
2. Click on the dispute for charge ch_3Xyz.
3. Click 'Submit evidence' and upload your tracking number and delivery confirmation screenshot.
4. Add a brief written explanation — for example: 'Tracking number [your number] confirms delivery on [date]. Delivery confirmation screenshot attached.'
5. Click 'Submit evidence' to send it to the card network before your deadline.

Tracking proof and delivery confirmation are among the strongest evidence types for this dispute reason. After you submit, the card issuer will typically take 60 to 75 days to evaluate your evidence and decide the outcome. I'll set an automated reminder on your case to follow up if you haven't confirmed submission within 48 hours.

learning.title: How to Respond to a Dispute in Your Stripe Dashboard
learning.subtitle: A step-by-step guide to submitting evidence and protecting your revenue when a chargeback is filed.
learning.summary: When a cardholder files a dispute, Stripe immediately reverses the payment and notifies the merchant. Merchants have a limited window — typically 7 to 21 days depending on the card network — to submit evidence before the deadline. This article explains the dispute lifecycle, what evidence to gather for each reason code, and how to submit a response in the Stripe Dashboard.
learning.content:
A dispute, also known as a chargeback, occurs when a cardholder questions a payment with their card issuer. When a dispute is created, the card network immediately reverses the payment — meaning the funds are removed from your Stripe balance while the dispute is under review. Acting quickly and submitting strong evidence is the most effective way to recover those funds.

Understanding the Dispute Timeline
After a dispute is opened, you have a limited time to respond to the card issuer — usually 7 to 21 days, depending on the card network. This deadline is firm: if you do not submit evidence before it expires, you automatically lose the dispute and cannot retrieve the funds. Stripe will notify you of the dispute via email and in your Dashboard, and the deadline will be displayed on the dispute detail page.

Step 1 — Identify the Dispute Reason Code
Every dispute has a reason code that tells you why the cardholder is disputing the charge. Common reason codes include 'product not received,' 'product not as described,' and 'fraudulent charge.' The reason code determines what evidence is most relevant. Navigate to Payments > Disputes in your Stripe Dashboard to find the reason code for your dispute.

Step 2 — Gather Your Evidence
For 'product not received' disputes, the strongest evidence includes: a tracking number showing the shipment was sent, carrier confirmation of delivery (including delivery date and address), any customer communication showing the order was acknowledged, and the order details including item description and fulfillment date. For 'product not as described' disputes, include photos of the item as shipped, your product description, and any customer communications. For 'fraudulent charge' disputes, include proof that the cardholder authorized the transaction, such as a signed receipt or IP address logs.

Step 3 — Submit Your Response in the Dashboard
In your Stripe Dashboard, go to Payments > Disputes and click on the relevant dispute. Click 'Submit evidence,' upload your supporting files, and add a written explanation summarizing your case. Be concise and factual — card network reviewers assess many disputes and clear, well-organized evidence is more persuasive. Click 'Submit evidence' to send your response before the deadline.

What Happens After You Submit
Once you submit evidence, the card issuer evaluates your submission and decides the outcome. This process typically takes 60 to 75 days, depending on the card network. Stripe will notify you of the outcome via email and in your Dashboard. If the dispute is decided in your favor, the reversed funds are returned to your Stripe balance. If the dispute is decided against you, the funds remain with the cardholder and a dispute fee is applied.

Preventing Future Disputes
The most effective way to reduce disputes is to use clear billing descriptors so customers recognize your charge on their statement, provide tracking information proactively, and respond quickly to customer inquiries. Stripe Radar, Stripe's fraud detection tool, can also help identify and block high-risk transactions before they result in disputes.

learning.title: Why Is My Payout on Hold? Common Causes and How to Resolve Them
learning.subtitle: Understand what triggers a Stripe payout hold and the steps to get your funds released.
learning.summary: Payout holds are one of the most urgent issues Stripe merchants face, as they can disrupt cash flow without warning. The most common triggers are incomplete account verification, a spike in disputes, or an unusual increase in transaction volume. This article explains each trigger, what Stripe needs from you to lift the hold, and how to avoid holds in the future.
learning.content:
A payout hold means Stripe has temporarily paused the transfer of funds from your Stripe balance to your bank account. Holds can feel alarming — especially when they coincide with a busy sales period — but most are resolved quickly once the underlying issue is addressed.

The Most Common Trigger: Verification Gaps
Stripe is required by financial regulations to verify the identity and legitimacy of every business it works with — a process known as Know Your Customer (KYC) verification. If your account is missing required information — such as business registration details, ownership information, a government-issued ID, or a verified bank account — Stripe may pause payouts until the information is provided and verified. Your Dashboard will typically indicate what information is needed under Settings > Account details.

Dispute Rate Spikes
A sudden increase in the number of disputes on your account can trigger an automated risk review. Card networks set thresholds for acceptable dispute rates, and when a merchant's rate approaches those thresholds, payment processors including Stripe are required to take action. If your dispute rate has spiked, Stripe may hold payouts while the risk team reviews your account. Resolving open disputes and demonstrating that you have addressed the root cause is the fastest path to lifting a dispute-related hold.

Unusual Volume Increases
A rapid, unexpected increase in transaction volume — for example, a viral promotion or a sudden influx of large orders — can trigger an automated review even if your dispute rate is normal. This is a standard fraud-prevention measure. Stripe's risk team will typically reach out via email to request additional information about the volume increase.

How to Resolve a Payout Hold
If your payouts are on hold, start by checking your Dashboard for any outstanding verification requirements or action items. Complete any requested document uploads promptly — blurry images, expired IDs, and name mismatches are common reasons verification stalls. If your Dashboard does not show a clear reason for the hold, open a support case with your account ID, the date the hold began, and your recent dispute rate. Providing this context upfront helps the support team investigate faster.

How Long Do Holds Last?
The duration of a payout hold depends on the cause. Verification-related holds are typically resolved within a few business days once complete documents are submitted. Risk-review holds may take longer depending on the complexity of the review. Stripe will notify you via email as the status of your hold changes.

Preventing Future Holds
Keep your account information up to date, including business address, ownership details, and bank account information. Monitor your dispute rate regularly in the Dashboard and address disputes promptly. If you anticipate a large volume spike — for example, due to a planned promotion — consider notifying Stripe in advance through your account settings or support channel.

learning.title: Understanding Stripe Billing: Proration, Subscription Upgrades, and Invoice Management
learning.subtitle: How Stripe Billing handles mid-cycle plan changes, proration credits, and invoice disputes for over 300,000 companies.
learning.summary: Stripe Billing manages nearly 200 million active subscriptions for more than 300,000 companies, supporting flexible pricing models including usage-based, tiered, and custom billing. When merchants or their customers upgrade or downgrade a subscription mid-cycle, Stripe applies proration logic that can result in immediate charges or credits. This article explains how proration works, how to view and dispute invoices, and how to manage subscription changes without surprises.
learning.content:
Stripe Billing is the subscription and invoicing engine used by more than 300,000 companies to manage nearly 200 million active subscriptions. Its flexibility — supporting usage-based, tiered, flat-rate, and custom pricing models — makes it powerful, but it also means that billing behavior during plan changes can be nuanced. Understanding how proration works is essential for avoiding unexpected charges and handling customer billing questions efficiently.

What Is Proration?
Proration is the process of adjusting a subscription charge to account for a mid-cycle plan change. When a customer upgrades to a higher-priced plan partway through a billing cycle, Stripe calculates the unused portion of the current plan and the cost of the new plan for the remaining days in the cycle. The difference is charged immediately, and the next full billing cycle begins at the new plan price. This means an upgrade mid-cycle typically results in an immediate partial charge rather than waiting until the next renewal date.

Why Did I Get Charged Immediately?
If you upgraded your plan and were charged right away, this is expected behavior under Stripe Billing's default proration settings. The immediate charge represents the prorated cost of the new plan for the remainder of the current billing period. Your next invoice at the start of the new cycle will reflect the full new plan price. If the charge amount seems incorrect, check your invoice in the Dashboard under Billing > Invoices — the line items will show the proration calculation in detail.

Billing Cycle Anchors
Stripe Billing uses a concept called a billing cycle anchor — the date on which your subscription renews each period. When you upgrade mid-cycle, the anchor date does not change; only the price and proration adjustment are applied. This means your renewal date stays the same, and the prorated charge bridges the gap between your old plan and your new plan for the current period.

How to View and Download Invoices
All invoices generated by Stripe Billing are available in your Dashboard under Billing > Invoices. Each invoice shows the line items, proration adjustments, tax (if applicable), and payment status. You can download invoices as PDFs for your records or share them with your finance team. If you use Stripe's Revenue Recognition or Tax products, additional reporting is available in the Dashboard.

Disputing a Billing Charge
If you believe a charge is incorrect — for example, if you were charged the full new plan amount instead of a prorated amount — open a support case with the invoice ID and subscription ID. Describe the expected charge and the actual charge so the support team can review the proration calculation. If a credit is warranted, the team can apply a credit note to your account, which will offset your next invoice.

Managing Downgrades and Cancellations
When a subscription is downgraded, Stripe Billing by default applies the change at the end of the current billing period rather than immediately, to avoid issuing a credit for unused time. Cancellations can be set to take effect immediately or at the end of the period, depending on your configuration. If you need to cancel immediately and receive a prorated refund, this requires a manual credit note or refund issued by your support team.
